newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia denies nuclear warheads theft.
newsitem.headline: Russia denies nuclear warheads theft.

text.p: Russian officials said on Monday Moscow had never had any atomic warheads stolen and dismissed a claim by a Russian disarmament expert who told a German newspaper that drunken workmen took two nuclear warheads in 1993.
"This is really idiotic. I have never heard anything more idiotic," Nikolai Yegorov, Russia's Deputy Atomic Energy Minister, told Reuters.

Sunday's Frankfurter Allgemeine quoted Russian nuclear expert Vladimir Orlov as saying two drunken workers stole two warheads from a Urals factory for a bet in 1993 and hid them in a garage in a residential area.
It quoted Orlov, head of the Moscow Institute for Security and Politics, as saying it was the first time a nuclear weapon had been stolen.
Yegorov dismissed the newspaper's report and said no nuclear warheads had ever been stolen.
Alexander Pikayev, a nuclear expert at the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said there was little chance of such a theft taking place.

"Nuclear fuel, nuclear waste has been stolen in Russia -- and all, even minor thefts have been traced. Anything about stolen warheads would have hit the headlines long ago if it happened in 1993," he said.

"Some people here may be 'wise' enough to take away nuclear fuel in their pockets, but warheads are a bit too large to steal and to hide in a garage," he said, adding that control was very tight at military and military-industrial objects.
He said most stolen nuclear materials came either from nuclear power stations or scientific institutions.

Pikayev said the only known case involving theft of enough weapons-grade nuclear material to make a bomb was in August 1994, when German police seized 363 grams (12.8 ounces) of plutonium-239 from couriers on a flight to Munich from Moscow.
German experts said the plutonium probably came from a laboratory and not a warhead.
Since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991, Western governments have worried that material stolen in former Soviet bloc could put nuclear arms within reach of non-nuclear states.
Pikayev said there had been seven confirmed cases of theft of nuclear materials of varying seriousness, and it was not clear if all these cases involved materials of Russian origin.
In October 1992, 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) of uranium was stolen in Podolsk near Moscow.
In July 1993, thieves stole 1.8 kg (3.9 lb) of submarine fuel waste in the Murmansk region and 4.5 kg (9.9 lb) of uranium were taken from a shipping enterprise in northern Russia.

In May 1994, German police found 5.6 grams (0.18 ounces) of plutonium in a private garage, and another haul of 800 grams (1.7 lb) of uranium was seized in Germany in June 1994. Another 2.72 kg (5.9 lb) of uranium were found in Prague in December 1994.
Pikayev added there had been no serious known thefts since 1994 and security measures had been stepped up at all Russian objects handling nuclear materials under a joint Russian-U.S programme.
